subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POSTPONEMENT OF DEADLINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour relating to the announcement by the locomotive engineers that they will be going on strike at the first of the week, which I know is a matter of great concern to the minister as it is to all Canadians. Has the minister anything he can report on this problem?

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POSTPONEMENT OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. First of all I would like the House to note in a positive vein that at six or seven o'clock this morning the non-operating unions, representing 55,000 railway workers, signed an agreement subject to ratification, and that the engineers, with whom I met last evening, are resuming negotiations with the CNR and in all probability with the CPR as well later this afternoon, probably about 2.30.

April 1, 1971
Inquiries of the Ministry
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that all elements for a settlement are in place, and I can only remind the railways, as well as the unions, of their obligation to the people who are not directly represented at the bargaining table, the farmers and the other people affected by the slowdown or wildcatting who could be detrimentally affected by a long strike. The responsibility now lies on the railways as well as on the men to realize their obligation to the Canadian people.

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POSTPONEMENT OF DEADLINE
speechtext: In view of the optimism of the minister, has he approached the representatives of the engineers' union or, if not, would he do so with a view to examining the possibilities of a postponement of a strike in any event, since the minister seems to suggest that some settlement may be worked out? I ask this question in view of the very disastrous effects such a strike would have on the economy.

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POSTPONEMENT OF DEADLINE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think the suggestion is a reasonable one. It is one that has already occurred to us, but it would only be fruitful if between now and Sunday there are some obvious signs of progress. When I say I am optimistic, I mean I am optimistic in the sense that both sides are resuming negotiations. This thought had occurred to me and I shall repeat it to the union later today.

maintopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY ON KEEPING VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY FILLED
IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY ON KEEPING VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY FILLED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. In view of the fact that most types of grain stocks in store at Vancouver terminals are presently depleted and that if storage facilities had been filled at Vancouver loading could have continued for another week or ten days and all the ships in port could have been filled regardless of the strike, is the minister prepared to reassess his position with regard to keeping terminal storage filled?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ofto E. Lang (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY ON KEEPING VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY FILLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the position of the Wheat Board has been a most reasonable one. Their objective
April 1, 1971

has been to maintain stocks at Vancouver as close to 15 million bushels as possible. In their judgment this figure allows for the maximum efficient use of the terminals in order to get the high throughput that is required with the record loadings which are going on and are anticipated. The stocks remained at 15 million bushels until early in the year. At that time the beginnings of labour difficulties reduced the efficiency of the transportation of grain and lost, in the opinion of the Wheat Board, effectively one week's unloadings at Vancouver. But even as late as March 10, and notwithstanding these difficulties, stocks were at 12.3 million bushels of grain, apart from screenings, at that terminal. I think the Wheat Board is to be commended for doing what they have done in keeping stocks there and in keeping the terminals operating as efficiently as possible in those difficult circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY ON KEEPING VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY FILLED
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister who reports for the Wheat Board whether any extraordinary measures were taken to replenish and, indeed, to increase stocks of wheat to full capacity at Vancouver and west coast points in view of the difficulties with regard to railway negotiations which must have been apparent to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY ON KEEPING VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY FILLED
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. As difficulties occurred during the earlier months of this year, the Wheat Board, operating through the block system, alternated orders to the opposite railroad as required in an attempt to keep stocks up. This created some difficulties, however, and made it more difficult to put the required grain in place. Some particular kinds of grain are handled, by the nature of things, more by the Canadian National than by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and this creates particular difficulties. The Wheat Board tried in every way to adjust its shipping schedules to keep stocks as high as possible and to have the right stocks there to meet the vessels which were expected.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister in charge of the Wheat Board a supplementary question. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: IMPENDING STRIKE BY LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS-POLICY RESPECTING UTILIZATION OF VANCOUVER GRAIN STORAGE CAPACITY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I should first of all point out my reference to screenings, which is not an inconsiderable quantity. Sometimes some millions of bushels of capacity can be taken up in that way. The objective of the Wheat Board is to assure that stocks are at such levels that boats can be met and also in order that the terminals themselves can operate with maximum efficiency. We are facing a period of months, and have been, when we will be testing the capacity of the terminals to put grain through them, and it is therefore extremely important that stocks do not rise above levels which allow the most efficient operation of those terminals. In the opinion of the Wheat Board, that would be about 15 million bushels of grain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House are very pleased to see the high priority which has been given to this piece of legislation. It is important that it should be passed now, and I shall take only three or four minutes so as not to impede the progress of the bill.
First, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs I would like to say how much we missed the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Legault) who has been hospitalized as a result of a coronary. We hope he will soon be restored to good health. The hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), as vice-chairman of the committee, was able to substitute in a very commendable manner and to maintain the same decorum, the same spirit of co-operation and of non-partisanship that characterizes that committee.
The object of all members of the committee, as always, was to improve the lot of our veterans. After all, they are the people who gave of themselves in the cause of our country. The very best evidence of the correctness of the decision which Your Honour made when you suggested that these items be taken out of the estimates and introduced as three specific pieces of legislation, came when a very useful amplification of the legislation was given to the committee. The committee hearings provided an opportunity for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) to clarify some of the rather hazy clauses, and the results which their passage would have upon veterans. A lot of us did not know what was involved, and I am sure a great many of the veterans did not know either, at least to judge by the number of letters which all hon. members received from them.
The minister's presence was much appreciated. His statements were also greatly appreciated, particularly the one relating to veterans allowances. It was on that matter that a great deal of confusion originally existed. Veterans are now being asked to apply for old age security pensions and guaranteed income supplements. We wondered how this would affect their status as veterans. The thing that bothered a lot of people was that a veteran may now be forced to pay income tax on his old age security pension and supplement, whereas he was exempt from income tax on his war veterans allowance. In the committee the minister was not able to say whether, in fact,
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952 this would be the case. He said it would be up to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) to decide whether or not this portion of a veteran's income would still be exempt from income tax.
One other small point which was raised concerned the fact that under the proposed new arrangement a veteran cannot live outside Canada for a whole year. For example, if he happens to have good friends who are able to take him away for a long holiday, say to the southern United States, he must return to Canada to qualify for pension, as do all people under the old age security pension scheme.
There were some other minor benefits about which we were also concerned, but again I say that Your Honour's decision meant that specific legislation had to be introduced and this enabled members of the committee to be enlightened further on the subject. Having made these few comments, may I add that we in this party are more than willing to give third reading to these important pieces of legislation. Our only regret is that it took so long to have them introduced. Since it took so long, we think the proposed benefits should be made retroactive to January 1, 1971, instead of coming into force on April 1, as is now the case.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with my namesake, the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), in expressing our regret at the illness of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Legault). We all wish him an early and speedy recovery.
Your Honour will recall that on Wednesday, March 10, when you ruled on a point of order having to do with the use of dollar items to effect certain kinds of legislation, you expressed the hope that although your ruling was going to make it necessary to have three separate bills introduced, nevertheless, since these matters related to veterans, the House would expedite the handling of this legislation. I can assure you that you expressed at that time the view of members generally. We dealt with this legislation expeditiously in Committee and are most anxious that there be no delay whatsoever in putting into effect the three bills, third reading of which we are dealing with this afternoon.
As the House is aware, we have already given third reading to Bill C-232, to amend the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, without debate, and unless somebody upsets the understanding the same will happen to Bill C-234, the bill to amend the Pension Act. But some of us feel that with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act amending bill, there are a few things that should be said. Since I have indicated that we are not debating the other two bills, perhaps I might be permitted just to say that we welcome the 10 per cent increase in disability pensions provided in the next bill. We wish it were more, but we know that at this stage of the game the chances of getting an increase are not enhanced by further debate. That is why we are giving our approval to the other two bills without debate.

April 1, 1971
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952
However, with respect to the changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act, although we welcome the increase of 15 per cent in the amount that can be paid as an allowance to war veterans allowance recipients, there are some ancillary things that have been done which we do not like and some things that ought to have been done which are not before us. What is happening is that the maximum amount that can be paid in the case of a single war veterans allowance recipient is being raised by 15 per cent from $105 a month to $121 a month. In the case of a married recipient, it is being raised from $175 a month by 15 per cent to the new figure $201 a month. In the case of these increases, it is roughly 15 per cent or it is 15 per cent, in round figures.
When it came to adjusting the ceilings on permissible income however, remembering that these allowances are under a means test, the government did not raise the ceilings by 15 per cent but only by the same dollar amount as the increases in the allowances themselves. The result is that the increase in the permissible income for a single war veterans allowance recipient is only 11 per cent and for a married recipient it is only 10 per cent. I should like to point out also that the amount of other income that a war veterans recipient can earn and still draw the full war veterans allowance is less than it was a number of years ago. We do not like that; we think the move should be in the other direction.
When the minister announced the changes on December 2, 1970, I pointed out that one of the effects of the new ceilings on the war veterans allowance payments, and the new provisions under the guaranteed income supplement, is that the preferential position of veterans on the war veterans allowance as compared with civilian pensioners has been narrowed. Under the former legislation a single war veterans allowance recipient could have, as a combination, $145 a month. At that point the ceiling for a person on the guaranteed income supplement was $105 a month. In other words, the single war veterans allowance recipient enjoyed a preference of $40 a month. Now, however, the ceiling on the income that a single war veterans allowance recipient can have is $161 a month, and the maximum under the old age security and guaranteed income supplement is $135 a month, so the difference is only $26 a month. In other words, the single war veterans allowance recipient who is unable to work and has no other income now has an advantage, and most of us in this House think he should have an advantage over the non-veteran, of $14 a month less than was the case before these two pieces of legislation were changed.
Under the former setup the married war veterans allowance recipient could receive $245 a month; under the guaranteed income supplement it was $210 a month or a spread of $35. That has been reduced. Now, the maximum permissible income under the War Veterans Allowance Act will be $271 a month as opposed to $225 a month combined old age security and guaranteed income supplement. In other words, the married war veterans

allowance recipient's preference has been reduced from $35 a month to $16 a month. I think I am quite justified in saying that in these cases veterans are being short changed. They are being given $14 less preference if single and $19 less if married. I do not think the people of Canada feel that we should short change our veterans that way.
These matters, Mr. Speaker, relating to the income that war veterans may have and still receive the war veterans allowance, are not covered directly by statute. The Statute permits the war veterans allowance board to deal with them by regulation and many of the changes to which I object have been made by regulation. I protest that the new ceilings were not made higher, and I protest that the preference for veterans was not at least maintained. Many of us in this House would like to go much further, but I think it is unfortunate that this change for the worse is being made. I know there are some on the government side who will ask what we are complaining about since veterans are going to get more money. But other people are getting more money, too, and I think we have a duty to our veterans that is not fully discharged by short-changing them in this way.
My friend, the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) has already referred to some of the results flowing from a decision made by the war veterans allowance board and concurred in by the Governor in Council. This is something over which we have no control in Parliament. The decision was that war veterans allowance recipients from now on must apply for the guaranteed income supplement if they are aged 65 or over. Some may ask if there is a law that forces people to apply. The fact is that a regulation has been passed to the effect that if they do not apply for the guaranteed income supplement they will be regarded as having applied and their war veterans allowance will be cut back accordingly.
Some may argue that it makes no difference, that in the end the ceiling is the effective figure, that a single war veterans allowance recipient ends up with $161 a month and a married war veterans allowance recipient ends up with $271 a month whether it is made up of OAS and WVA or OAS, GIS and WVA. That is quite true; the ceilings in the War Veterans Allowance Act are the determining factors on how much income will be received. But there are a number of other factors that veterans do not like and I share their point of view.
Perhaps the first factor is psychological, but a psychological factor can be very real. Veterans like to feel that what is being done for them, if it is not a matter of right as it is under the Pension Act and if there has to be a means test proposition as there is under the War Veterans Allowance Act, at least is being done under war veterans legislation. For them to be told to move over to the kind of legislation that is general welfare is not what they were led to believe would be their lot when they enlisted in the armed forces. I do not think it is right to tell these people that they must move over to the welfare side, rather than getting what is their due under veterans legislation.
April 1, 1971

In addition to the psychological disadvantage that veterans feel flows from this change, there are a few other things. The previous speaker has already referred to the income tax situation. I know that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) is not in a position to disclose income tax secrets, not even in a meeting of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He could tell us what is in the white paper on taxation with which we are all familiar but, in effect, he asked us to believe that when it becomes legislation veterans will not be taxable because they have been moved over to the guaranteed income supplement. I say that is a pig-in-a-poke. We do not know what is going to happen in terms of income tax reform; we do not know what the figures are going to be. Certainly for the month of April the income tax law is such and the exemption levels are such that veterans, having been put on old age security and the guaranteed income supplement, will find that their income is subject to income tax, and their net income will thus be reduced. On the other hand, if a reasonable portion of a veteran's income were made up of veterans allowances, that would not be taxable income. Until such time as the income tax law is changed, this will be the picture and veterans will face the possibility or probability of paying income tax, and thus receiving a reduced net income, as a result of this government's action in forcing them to apply for the guaranteed income supplement. This I do not like.
Another element came out in the meeting of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs yesterday. I think, in this respect, that I must say the minister met our point. When he asks the House to believe something that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will do, he is asking us to buy a pig-in-a-poke. But when he tells us what he will do, I feel that he is speaking for himself. I refer to the fact that we complained that the benefit of the 2 per cent annual escalation that has taken place in the guaranteed income supplement which has been given to war veterans allowance recipients was being stopped. The minister said at the end of that discussion that there was no reason to believe it was stopped for all time. I plead that he make that a commitment. He and I already have made a bargain, to the effect that if he does not keep that commitment he can expect questions and late show debates next year to see that it is done.
At present the married veteran, let us say, gets a total of $271 as a result of getting the OAS and GIS, plus a little bit of the war veterans allowance. One year from now he can have his old age security and guaranteed income supplement increased by 2 per cent; but as the law now stands, unless something is done, the amount that he would get by way of an increase on the one hand would be taken out of the other. It would be taken away from his war veterans allowance, because the ceiling is $271. I say, quite readily, that the minister asked us to believe yesterday that he would not let that situation obtain next year. 1 accept his assurance in that matter. The law does not help us at this point. I plead that there be no cases next year of veterans having their war
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952
veterans allowance payments reduced to offset the increase that they get by way of an escalation in their old age security and guaranteed income supplement payments.
There was another area about which we had a good deal of discussion in the committee yesterday. Possibly hon. members will remind me that we went around in circles. We cannot do that in the House of Commons because we are only permitted to speak once. I am thinking of what is being done in respect of widows of war veterans allowance recipients. As the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) pointed out, there has been considerable confusion concerning benefits that veterans lose when they come off the war veterans allowance. It does not take very much extra income to make a veteran ineligible for war veterans allowance. A veteran may be getting the old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement. The war veterans allowance he can get, if he has nothing else, is only $26 a month in the case of a married veteran and only $16 a month in the case of a single veteran. Any veteran who has other income, say a small civil service pension, a pension from some other source, an annuity or what have you, may become completely ineligible for the war veterans allowance.
We were concerned about this, and concerned that this would result in the loss of all ancillary benefits available to a veteran being paid the war veterans allowance. The minister made it clear in a statement yesterday that there are two benefits which will not be lost. One of those would be the benefit under the treatment regulations and the other under the burial regulations, if you can call that a benefit, which you do not lose. The minister made it clear that if a veteran required treatment, he could get it, just as if he were in receipt of the war veterans allowance. If he is not on the war veterans allowance because he is getting the guaranteed income supplement, he will get the treatment, and that benefit will be available to him as long as he lives. That is good. He also made it clear that if a veteran is not receiving war veterans allowance because he is receiving the guaranteed income supplement, and that veteran dies, no matter whether that is one year from now or 20 or 30 years from now, he will be given the benefit of the burial regulations just as if he had been on the war veterans allowance. That is good, too.
Now, we come to the position of the potential widow. We were informed yesterday-and all this, I point out, has been done under the regulations governing the War Veterans Allowance Act-that if a veteran, who is not in receipt of war veterans allowance by reason of his being on the guaranteed income supplement, dies within a year of the time when he went off the war veterans allowance-and I emphasize that deadline-the widow will get the same consideration that she would have been given if the veteran had been in receipt of war veterans allowance. That brings to her one very important benefit, the married rate for a full year. But if he dies after a year has passed from the time when he went off the war veterans allowance, then she does not get that benefit at all. She may still have the rights that all other widows of

April 1, 1971
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952
veterans have, the right to a widow's allowance under the War Veterans Allowance Act, but the particular right giving her one year's benefit at the married rate is taken away from the widow of a veteran who went off the veterans allowance more than one year before he died.
Today is April 1, the day when the new legislation comes into effect. Therefore, effective as of today, many veterans will no longer receive the war veterans allowance. Many of those veterans are married. If any such veteran dies during the next 12 months, his widow will get the benefit of one year's allowance at the married rate. If however, one of those veterans who is to come off the allowance today were to die 13 or 14 months from now, his widow would not get the benefit of the married rate for the full year. Granted that the allowance is only a stop-gap for one year, it is a right which has been of great assistance to many widows. Granted that she has the other rights, and so on; I know all the arguments we went into yesterday about putting people over 65 in the same position as those between 60 and 65, and so on. The fact of the matter is that we are taking something away that existed for years. We are taking away a right that was good and I do not think that should be done. It will not be necessary to bring in legislation to make this change. It can be done by regulation. I hope that one year from now, when complaints start coming in and other hon. members start asking questions, the minister will reconsider this whole matter and change the regulations to maintain for widows the same benefits that are available to them now.
I confess that the whole operation is one I do not like, and I have already said so. The operation of pushing veterans from the War Veterans Allowance Act to the guaranteed income supplement, which I think could quite properly be defined as being in the area of general welfare, I do not like.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: The war veterans allowance is welfare.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) says that the War Veterans Allowance Act is a welfare measure. That is quite true. But it is a welfare measure for veterans, whereas the other is a welfare measure for the general population. As I tried to say when making my first point, it means something to veterans, even though some of them may have to go on welfare, if they are covered by their own legislation instead of by the general legislation.
I believe we should be moving in the other direction. In these days of unemployment all sorts of suggestions are being made. One of them is that, in order to permit more employment opportunities for young people, older people should retire earlier. In my view, this idea is sound, and I think we ought to make a start in the area of veterans and make it possible for veterans, because they are veterans, to retire early. A war veterans allowance program or special pensions for veterans at 55 or even 50 is the direction in which we should be moving. Instead, we are
narrowing such welfare benefits as are already provided and I register my protest.
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldi-mand, I am glad to see this 15 per cent increase in war veterans allowances. I wish it were more. I am glad to see the 10 per cent increase that will come in the bill that follows, which we do not plan to debate at the third reading stage. But I plead with the minister to do a great deal more in recasting these regulations to give our veterans the full benefits that I believe the Canadian people would like this Parliament to give to them.

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on Bill C-233 now before the House which deals with war veterans allowances.
I fully agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As a matter of fact, he has dealt with this matter in a very detailed manner with the adroitness of a master.
Mr. Speaker, we are very happy to find that the government has yielded to the pressures of war veterans and is giving them a little more justice, because they certainly have rights and prerogatives which must be considered in order to take the required decisions.
I fully appreciate the decisions of the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) and I should like to congratulate him heartily for his courage and his openmindedness in doing justice to this oppressed social class.
We are happy that the government should grant these pension settlements which represent an approximate amount of $43 million, part of which will be absorbed by old age pensions.
Mr. Speaker, this is money just the same. Money paid out as old age security pensions even if it does not come out of the budget of the Department of Veterans Affairs, is still money. So, this will cost the Treasury $43 million more.
It is not the veterans' fault nor the hon. members' fault; but that of the system if the cost of living has increased and pensions and grants have to be increased again and again. There is no end to this. Everything increases, and eventually taxes have to be increased too.
I am glad that veterans' pensions are being increased, but I am dissatisfied that we have to increase taxes accordingly to pay our veterans what is rightfully theirs.
However, I agree concerning our veterans and all those who have given much of themselves, who have made countless sacrifices, and who have forsaken part of their existence to save the nation and to establish a certain priority with respect to justice and freedom in our society. They are the ones who fought for that. I still wonder though whether they were justified in doing so but, in any case, it was for the sake of freedom, of civilization, of Christianity, that they sacrificed part of their lives and

April 1, 1971

it is for the sake of all that also that we have increased their pensions.
Such increases cost money but still there are other groups of citizens in Canada who have needs that ought to be fulfilled, who would require increases in pension or income but there are only tax increases for them.
We must be fair and ensure equal opportunity in all of this. The increase in pension which is offered the war veterans by the minister of Veterans Affairs will draw their gratitude, all the more so since other citizens who also have the right to live are victims of certain disadvantages forced on them by the economic system.
I would like once again to state my admiration for the wonderful work done by the minister, and also by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knnowles) who fights so well for the rights of the veterans, of the oppressed and of all those who are in need. I support him in his demands, even though we live in a system where we must often limit ourselves.
I believe, therefore, that the veterans will understand the situation and will be that much more satisfied with what the government grants them. We hope therefore that with higher pensions they will be a little happier, because while receiving a little more from the state, they will see that the latter saw their problems and decided not to forget them.

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
As the hon.
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) have said, there will not be a protracted debate on these three bills. I join with the two hon. members in wishing my colleague, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Legault), a speedy recovery.

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
I stated yesterday in committee that I visited the chairman of this committee in hospital when he was quite ill, but it was not possible to go into his room. Notwithstanding this, he sent out the message that there were three pieces of veterans' legislation that he was most anxious to see passed. That is the measure of the hon. member for Nipissing.
Some of the points made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are well taken. The fact that the minister has brought forth these splendid pieces of legislation speaks well of him. The nitty-gritty attacks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, some of which I support, must not serve as a smoke screen to hide what is, in effect, three splendid pieces of legislation. I believe they will put an additional $40 million to $50 million in the hands of these veterans.
I was very pleased yesterday to receive a letter from the Royal Canadian Legion asking that this bill be passed as expeditiously as possible. I thank the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand for his kind comments on the manner in which I chaired the committee yesterday. My job was
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952
made much easier by having been a member of this committee under two former capable chairmen, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) and the hon. member for Nipissing. I was also assisted by the fact that these are three pieces of good legislation. More important, we received the complete co-operation of the opposition members sitting on that committee.
This piece of legislation should and will be passed expeditiously because all members of this House want to ensure that the veterans receive justice. I say to the veterans, do not rest on your laurels because of these three great pieces of legislation. Be ever vigilant and keep our committee informed of the improvements you would like to see in this and new legislation.

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only propose to make a very few brief remarks on this important piece of legislation because, although I do not like to admit it, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already made most of the speech I would have made under these circumstances. We have similar views on a number of subjects which I find important and the hon. member has covered them carefully and accurately, so I do not propose to be repetitive.
However, I do want to say that all members of the Veterans Affairs Committee regret the fact that our very capable chairman, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Legault), was unable, for health reasons, to be present while these bills were being considered. We wish him a rapid and complete recovery. At the same time we express our appreciation to the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) for filling in so capably as chairman of the Veterans Affairs Committee.
I have been a member of this committee from time to time over the last 20 years or so, and I might say it is a committee that has functioned on a non-partisan basis. It is one that recognizes, regardless of party affiliation, one mutual concern of all its members, and that is that the veterans of the country who have fought in World Wars I and II, the Korean war and some other minor military engagements should be treated in the way that Canadians generally felt they should be treated at the time of these crises.
I regret one aspect of consideration that is given to the war veterans allowance legislation. It is true there is a philosophy that because of their service veterans age prematurely, and that war veterans allowance is, in fact, an old age pension that the veterans receive at an earlier age than is the case with civilians. However, as years go by it seems a grateful nation-if that nation is accurately represented by this government-wants to forget its obligation to the veterans as such. There seems to be a tendency to hope that the veterans will fade away into the general age group to which they happen to belong, and that their needs will be looked after by the general benefits available to all citizens within that age group.
I think this is a very unfortunate attitude to adopt. We are seeing the relative benefits that our veterans have

April 1, 1971
War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952
had under veterans legislation being eroded in several ways. For example, old age pension was payable at the age of 70; war veterans allowance was payable in a general sense at the age of 60. The veteran had a ten-year advantage. The old age pension recipient now receives the old age pension at the age of 65, the age having been lowered from 70 to 65. But there has been no corresponding lowering of the qualifying age for war veterans allowance.
Then, as has already been pointed out, it would seem there is a desire on the part of the government, where the benefit is a similar one, to treat the veteran as a civilian in cases where he has an option between either the old age security and income supplement or the war veterans allowance.
War veterans allowance carries with it a number of subsidiary benefits. But the most important point of all is that the veteran feels he receives war veterans allowance as of right. Even if it is in the form of a welfare payment to which is attached a means test, he still looks upon it as something to which he is entitled because he served in the armed forces in time of war. He receives it only because he served in two world wars, either in Canada or in an actual theatre of war overseas. He may be in receipt of a very small disability pension to compensate him for the deterioration in his health due to illness or to wounds sustained during his military service. But as I say, he looks upon his war veterans allowance with pride, as something that sets him apart from the ordinary citizen.
I think the veteran resents having his pension replaced by old age security and the general income supplement, even if his total monetary benefit is unchanged. There are a number of fringe benefits to which a veteran is entitled. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) listed these so accurately that I will not repeat them now, but I should like to say this: Most of these benefits are either dispensed or withdrawn by regulation. I should like to impress upon the minister, as forcibly as I can, that in cases where a veteran is in receipt of old age security, the income supplement plus some small additional third source of income, which thus disqualifies him from receiving war veterans allowance, none of the fringe benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled should be taken away from him, regardless of what these are.
Further, I strongly recommend that in every case where regulations such as those enumerated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre apply, they be amended so that war veterans are placed in no worse position in receiving the old age security pension and the income supplement than they were when their income was derived from the taxpayers through the Department of Veterans Affairs. I see no reason why the veterans, who have their own department as it were, should not have all their needs met by that department. This would mean a corresponding reduction in expenditure on the part of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I submit the government should refrain from attempting to make the old veterans fade away into the general age group of the population into which they happen to fall.

maintopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT, 1952 AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TABLE AND CEILING OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has very adequately covered the questions relating to war veterans allowance but I did want to make a few points in respect of a problem that is not being resolved in this legislation, namely the lowering of the qualifying age for widows of veterans for war veterans allowance.
It seems to me that there is a very solid principle here, and it is this. The capacity of men who have served in the armed forces in a theatre of war, and have suffered disability therefrom, to earn their own living and to make adequate provision for their families has undoubtedly been impaired. Yet if their disability is not in excess of 50 per cent of their total capacity, or if their death is not due to war service, their widows are ineligible for war veterans allowance unless they are 55 years or over, or unless they are medically unfit. I am not quarrelling with the minister or his department about the decisions which have been handed down, because under the Act and under the regulations, these are the decisions required. But I hope the minister will be prepared to give consideration to lowering the age at which the widow of a veteran would be eligible for war veterans allowance.
Here is an example which illustrates what I have in mind, the case of a woman who is the widow of a Canadian serviceman who served in the Korean war. Her husband, I understand, was the first Canadian to be wounded in that theatre of war. When he returned to Canada he was granted a 15 per cent disability pension. His disability undoubtedly affected his earning capacity and resulted in the deterioration of his health to the point where he was scheduled for reboarding at a hearing which would probably have resulted in his disability pension being increased. He had come to the point where he realized he would have to quit the heavy work he was doing and seek lighter employment. Unfortunately, he was killed in a car accident, leaving a widow and a young son to face the future without adequate means of support.
The department, under the regulations and terms of the act, ruled that this woman was not eligible for a pension unless she was proven to be medically unfit. She was not medically unfit. The case was appealed to the appeal board which pointed out that she was not eligible, first, because she was only 50 years of age, and second, because she was neither permanently unemployable nor incapable of maintenance. It is true, I suppose that in physical terms a woman 50 years of age is not permanently unemployable or incapable of maintenance, but in actual fact, where does a woman of 50 years of age, without any particular training, get a job to maintain herself and her child? True, she can get odd days clerking in a store or do housework for someone on a day to day basis, but it is virtually impossible for her to maintain herself and her child adequately. This means that the particular woman I have in mind will be forced, eventually, to go on welfare.

April 1, 1971

As a Canadian, I resent the fact that the widow of a man who was wounded while serving his country should be required to go on welfare. Given the circumstances of today, there is real justification for lowering the age of eligibility from 55 to 50 or even to 45. If we were in a period when it was easy to get jobs, when there was a demand for labour, this difficulty might not arise. But today there are thousands of young people looking for jobs, and the chances of a widow, 50 years of age, without any particular skills, securing employment, are virtually nil.
If the minister and the government want to face the realities of the present situation, then surely they ought to give consideration to lowering the age from 55 to 50. Not only do we have a responsibility to veterans but we have a responsibility to the families of veterans. The average veteran I talk to is more concerned about the people of Canada discharging their responsibility to veterans' families than they are about veterans themselves. When I talked to veterans in the last war, my impression was they were worried not so much about what would happen to them as about what would happen to their families if they failed to come back or if they came back in an incapacitated condition. I think the widow of a man who served his country in a theatre of war, who suffered a serious disability, deserves something from this nation; we have a responsibility toward her and her children.
The other thing I should like to say to the minister is this. I hope he will be giving serious consideration fairly soon, since he is not going to do it in the legislation before us, to providing for a cost of living bonus in war veterans allowances and disability pensions. We are already accepting this principle in connection with pension plans, superannuation plans for civil servants, the Canada Pension Plan the old age security pension provisions when combined with the guaranteed income supplement. If, in all these programs, we recognize that an increase in the cost of living automatically reduces the purchasing power of a pension, I see no reason why we should not accept the same principle with respect to those who are in receipt of veterans disability pensions or war veterans allowances. I am pleased that the benefit of doubt rule has finally received full attention. If this rule is followed properly, many of the things which have bothered veterans and the friends of veterans will disappear. The Veterans Affairs Committee has been active over the years. You often hear on some corner, not too often but sometimes, the argument that we have done too much for veterans. I am glad to see the minister does not feel that way and that the committee does not feel that way. If there are people who still have this idea, I might mention the fact that the veterans rehabilitation program we had after the war apparently cost a good deal of money, but this money has been repaid to the nation many times over in the form of income tax. Many of these veterans returned to school after they came home. It is true they did so through the generosity of the taxpayers, but they did have a desire to upgrade themselves. They showed us that they did not want to rest on their laurels as veterans but wished to get back into the stream of life. A great many of these veterans distinguished themselves in college. I understand they were the best students the faculty had. They were not busy burning down schools or asking for something for nothing. Through income tax they have paid back the people of Canada many times the full cost of the veterans rehabilitation program. If we traced it through, I believe we would find they have paid back the full cost of the veterans programs up to the present day.
I do not think we have reached the end of the road in respect of veterans affairs. There are still a few untidy corners to be cleaned up. The Committee on Veterans Affairs will have to be kept together and revitalized. This committee has always had fine chairmen. The last two in particular have been outstanding, although they are not alone in this regard because there were very fine chairmen before them. I do not think we have succeeded completely in giving proper attention to those veterans with multiple disabilities. I am pleased there has been a breakthrough, but I am quite sure improvements are required in this regard.
I am not too happy that there has been no change in the attitude in respect of the provisions concerning misconduct, particularly where a widow is deprived of a pension because of some presumed misconduct on the part of the serving member. If the benefit of doubt rule had been properly applied in the old days it would have looked after the situation, but this was not the case. Mr. Speaker, I wish to limit my brief remarks on Bill C-233 to the increase in the war veterans allowance. I regret that when bringing in a bill to amend the act in order to increase the rates, the minister did not take to heart the suggestion I put to him, I thought rather vehemently, in respect of those veterans who I believe are unjustly being denied access to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I should like the Minister to give careful consideration to this point. I refer particularly to those veterans of World War I and World War II living in the United Kingdom who, because they have not put in one year's residence in Canada since the war or since their war service, are not entitled to apply. I cannot think of any greater discrimination than this particular restriction. I have repeated this suggestion time and time again. We have been given the answer that there are administrative or bureaucratic difficulties dealing primarily with Canadians who live in the United States. The benefits to Canadian veterans living in the United States, under whatever entitlement they may have, are in excess of what they might get in Canada or at least that was the case in the past. So, we were given an artificial reason for it being impossible to pay these men.
I invite the minister to really look into the case of those veterans who are residing in the United Kingdom. I am sure he has received briefs and letters from the Canadian Veterans Association of the United Kingdom and also personal representations from persons who had been officers in the department in the United Kingdom as well as from Canadian veterans who were in London and who are aware of the hardship. Yet, for some unknown reason we have had a continuation of the refusal to consider these people as being eligible. I say there is an omission from this bill because it would have been very simple to include an amendment to rectify this situation. My regret is that despite all the good things that have been done, not only under Bill C-203 but under these three particular bills dealing with an increase in the rates, the minister has failed to do something for these people. There are other cases in respect of which I could make suggestions, but in this particular case I say there has been a very serious omission and I would hope we could see our way clear before long to make the change.
As we all know there is the difficulty that once both the Pensions Act and the War Veterans Allowances Act have been amended in a major way, the administration will have a closed mind with regard to re-opening these acts. We will be put off for perhaps another five years before any change is made. I can think of circumstances under which it might happen much quicker, but if one follows the present thinking any further changes will take that long. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, this is one point on which I can tell the minister I will keep dogging him until I see some hope of improvement in this situation. I hope it is not the position of the department that by just hanging tough they will wear out this category of veterans through the passage of time, because many of them now are on in years.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill was introduced for first reading one could definitely hear the strains of that old Liberal theme song being played in the background, a song we are all so familiar with, "Roll out the barrel." There is no doubt what that barrel contains. It is the old-fashioned Liberal pork barrel, because this clause we are dealing with is nothing more or less than the introduction of patronage on a grand scale.
We are being asked, under the provisions of this clause, to authorize the establishment of five ministers of state. This means that if the clause is passed, the government would be quite justified in establishing, without further reference to Parliament, five new departments, and without demonstrating any need whatsoever for any one of them. When you realize that the cost of doing the work which these new departments will do, over and above what it is costing now to do that same work in the existing departments, will be untold millions of dollars each year, untold millions that the taxpayer must pay,

April 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
then you have to look very carefully at what we are being asked to approve in this clause.
When you establish a single new department you establish a new minister, deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers, associate deputy ministers, and a whole host of directors at high salaries. Then, there are large public relations staffs employed as image makers, many of whom are lured from the press gallery. Heaven knows the image of the ministers needs building up but not at public expense. As well, you have private secretaries, associate private secretaries, assistant private secretaries, executive assistants, parliamentary secretaries and all the paraphernalia that goes with a separate department. We know from experience that these things cost the taxpayer millions of dollars, and in the end exactly the same amount of work is done.
We must ask why this proposal is being made at this time, Mr. Chairman. I say it is being made for one reason and one reason alone. The government will not wait until the need for a new department can be justified, rather it comes with this proposition now in order to provide opportunities for the Liberal faithful, the elected and the party workers.
A good example of how this works, Mr. Chairman, happened in 1963. The chief organizer of the Liberal party, Mr. Walter Gordon, had promised that he would provide jobs galore to the Liberal faithful so he set up the Department of Industry. There was no more need for that separate department than there was for a hole in the head, Mr. Chairman. The work had previously been done by the industrial section of the Department of Trade and Commerce. A brand new department was established in its own separate building with a minister, deputy minister and all the other paraphernalia costing the taxpayers many millions of dollars.
Before 1963 the work of this new department had been looked after by the industrial section of the Department of Trade and Commerce in a most satisfactory and efficient manner, as will be obvious to anybody who has talked to the businessmen of Canada. It took three times as many people to staff the new department, however, as had run the industrial section. A great many of the new staff members were high priced directors from every facet of industrial life-they were recruited in hordes. The new department cost untold millions of dollars each year to operate.
Then, why was this new department finally disbanded and put back exactly where it had been prior to the election of 1963? It was for a very simple reason. The businessmen of Canada became so frustrated and furious with the confusion of having to deal with two departments instead of one that they demanded this nonsense to be stopped. The government had to swallow its pride and put the Department of Industry back into the Department of Trade and Commerce.
As any businessman knows, Mr. Chairman, firms which export also produce for the domestic market and most producers for the domestic market also sell to the export
market to help cover their overhead, to increase profits and sometimes to reduce their prices. Anybody knows that. You do not have one group of people producing for export who want to deal with an export department, and another group producing only for domestic consumption who want to deal with the Department of Industry. All companies of any size want to deal with just one department. Prior to 1963 they were able to do this and were happy about it. I challenge any member of the House to tell me one incident of a businessman who was not extremely happy with the operation of the Department of Trade and Commerce, both from the point of view of export sales and domestic industry. The division of this department into two was done solely to provide patronage jobs for the Liberal faithful.
We in the opposition are doing everything we can to persuade the government to stop this nonsense at public expense. Even when a department is split in order to provide jobs for the party faithful and then is brought back to the original position, the waste does not stop. It did not stop when the Department of Trade and Commerce was divided. When the businessmen of this country forced the marriage of these two departments again, this government did not let out a single employee of the Department of Industry. Since that time they have been falling over each other and getting in each other's way, causing inefficiency and confusion. The businessmen of the country are not as happy with the operation of the department as they were prior to 1963. You cannot right a wrong by bringing the two departments back together.
This government, Mr. Chairman, has no right to ask this Parliament for a blank cheque to create five new departments for which it cannot justify the need. If it could justify the need, the government ought to come before Parliament and say what that need is. Instead, it is asking Parliament for a blank cheque. The government wants to spend literally hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayer's money on changes that are not justified. They are not needed and they are only excuses for providing jobs for the faithful. As another election approaches, we see the old pork barrel coming out again. The government is saying, "Boy, we are creating five new departments and all sorts of jobs for you if you get elected. We will make you parliamentary secretaries; we will make you ministers; we will make you almost anything you want; but run and win. Come in and join the Liberal party. Help us to win, because we love power and we want to enjoy it."

speechtext:
I apologize, Mr. Chairman, I wanted to give my friends an opportunity to say all they had to say so that they might in turn show the same courtesy we apply to them, in other words, listen.
Yesterday I was speaking on Part IV of Bill C-207 concerning the establishment of ministries of state and appointment of the corresponding number of ministers of state, or a maximum of five.
At that time, my major argument was to determine the links between the three separate powers which govern Canada, i.e. the judiciary, executive and legislative powers.
My remarks were rather academic and I was suggesting that when one of the powers wants to arrogate certain rights of the two other powers, serious conflicts occur with far-reaching effects for the powers involved.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw the attention of the committee to more general considerations. For example, I would like to know what the government is trying to achieve in establishing ministries of state. It is said in Part IV of this bill that the government is proposing the establishment of "ministries of state for specified purposes".
Now, upon reading the relevant clauses, one becomes aware that the purposes mentioned in the title are not included in Part IV of the legislation. This is an incomprehensible shortcoming which is greatly responsible for the imbroglio this House is in now.
Now, I wonder, why does the government want to create ministries of state without telling us what fields
April 1, 1971

they will cover? Why not say what these ministries will do, or what problems they will deal with?
Mr. Chairman, the government does not give its reasons. It would like to have the overall authority to create ministries of state at will, for reasons it does not want to reveal. This is a dangerous principle, because the House not only does not know why certain amounts of money are spent, but it does not know if these ministries will endeavour to solve the problems it might want to refer to them.
Thus, the government is asking for a blank cheque, without revealing its reasons, without stating its intentions. It is useless to say that we object to this scheme.
As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) stated yesterday, when he took part in this debate, Canada is an over-governed country. There is no dearth of directors in Canada! There is a profusion of ministers and parliamentary secretaries who keep themselves busy doing we do not know exactly what. When they are asked questions about what is going on in their departments or about their position or policy in any specific area, their answers are evasive, vague or else facetious. If serious answers are needed to serious questions, the situation is hopeless, they cannot be obtained.
This goes to show once again to what extent this government is making Parliament look ridiculous. For sure, there are departments that are doing a good job. Let us take for instance the department of the Secretary of State. What sort of information can we get out of this department? Whenever a member of the opposition directs a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), the latter always unmistakably begins like this: Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of this, but I shall look into it. Mr. Speaker, I am not responsible for this, but I shall inquire. Mr. Speaker, I did not know this, I have not been informed of this problem, but I shall find out and report to the hon. member.
First of all, we always have to wait for the said reports, and then it is inconceivable that a minister of a responsible government should not be responsible for the CBC, for example, to Parliament. It is nonsensical.
Here is an example. Some people ask for the establishment of a commission. I call for the creation of a royal commission of inquiry into the CBC's activities in general. The Secretary of State rises and, as he is the minister responsible for this organization, replies: I am not responsible. The only part I have to play is to run errands between the government and the CBC.
As for parliamentary control, this means that hon. members of any party not only have no influence over the CBC, but must be content with what the Corporation is ready to give them, albeit ungraciously. So hon. members who must report to their constituents on the CBC's administration are unable to do so. They are handicapped in their informatory and participatory duties either because the responsible minister refuses to fulfil his obligations or because he is truly not the master at the CBC. Who then is the master of that Crown corporation that is financed through public funds if it is not the Secretary of State?
Government Organization Act, 1970
Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw the committee's attention to a specific point in the bill before us. If in the case of the CBC Parliament has no direct control over public funds, and if the Secretary of State who is responsible for this corporation does not control it either and does not know how the funds are spent, how can Parliament hope to have a control over ministers of state and ministries that Parliament will not even be asked to establish, or over ministers that Parliament will not be called upon to judge? Moreover, Parliament will be unable to properly assess the work of the ministers because the latter will not have to answer to Parliament.
That is how the executive weakens the legislative power so as to turn it into an ivory tower parallel to the legislative power, in such a way that some day, we will reach the point where parliament will be a tower of Babel where we will do nothing but talk, with no accounts to render to anyone.
On the other hand, there will be a unilateral, dictatorial power which will take decisions while ignoring what can be said in the tower of Babel, that is Parliament, and so our democratic institutions will keep on depreciating in the eyes of the public, particularly of the young people.
We all agree on rejuvenating Parliament and we want the executive power to have all means available to carry on effectively the task that the people have entrusted to it. But from that to squashing one power to the benefit of another, to neglecting to exercise parliamentary control over the various creatures of the government, it does not make sense.
We cannot normally operate with that system. At the present time, it is easier for government members to uphold their position and I understand them. However, if those same members who want to increase the executive power under the pretext of making it more efficient were sitting on this side of the House, they would speak as we do. They would defend Parliament, because for them it would be the sole satisfactory institution to convey the representations of the people to the government. This is one of the basic reasons why Parliament exists.
As for the creation of ministries of state about which we did not obtain any specific information-my hon. friends opposite will admit it-we cannot honestly accept it. We have nothing-and we want it to be well understood-against the creation of ministries of state. We object to the motivation, the responsibilities and the power given to those ministries or ministers of state. We especially object to the eventual lack of relations between those ministers and Parliament.
Mr. Chairman, I deemed it important to once again bring up those issues during the debate with the hope of prompting the government members to change their minds about the creation of those ministries of state.
Mr. Chairman, we are not here to hinder the government in their business, but to help them. We are here to show them the dark side of the picture, which they may forget at times.

April 1, 1971

speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the report by C. B. Haver of Montreal for Northumberland Consultants Limited regarding a review of the cost-benefit evaluation by Stanford Research Institute for a Prince Edward Island causeway as mentioned in answer to Question Number 1,832 reported in Hansard, July 21, 1969 at page 11374.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think the motion I moved tor the production of papers, a request was rejected by the government, speaks for itself. What is involved here, as far as I am concerned, is the question of how governments make decisions, on what information they make them, how much of that information should be made available to the public in general, what information should be kept private and confidential, and what reasons the government has for keeping such information private and confidential.
The subject of building a causeway from Prince Edward Island to the mainland of Canada has been debated for many years. I will leave it to members from the Maritimes, and from Prince Edward Island in particular, to discuss in greater detail, and with a good deal more knowledge than I, the necessity for such a causeway and the advantages to be gained from its construction. Suffice it for me to say that it was a Liberal government that promised the people of Prince Edward Island that, if elected, it would proceed with the building of a causeway which would thus obviate the necessity for moving from Prince Edward Island to the mainland of Canada by way of the ferry.
Estimates were made of the cost of constructing such a causeway. I speak from memory, but I think I am not far wrong in saying that the original estimate given to the public was for an amount in the neighbourhood of $140 million to $150 million. Subsequently, the government announced that a new estimate, amounting to $200 million or more, had been made of the cost of constructing a crossing. The cost was so high, and the benefits to be derived so slight, that the government felt it could not proceed with the project. Whether the fact that an election had been held and the Liberal party had been singularly unsuccessful in electing members from Prince Edward Island was a factor that influenced the government's decision I leave to members of the Liberal party to discuss if they so see fit. But the fact is that the decision was made not to proceed to construct the crossing.
I am not here today to contend that the original proposal to build the causeway was correct. I am not here today to say that the subsequent decision not to build the causeway was incorrect. I am not here to say that if a causeway could have been built for $140 million it would
Prince Edward Island Causeway
have been proper to build it. I am not here to say that if the causeway cost twice $140 million it is too expensive, and that we should not proceed with its construction. What I am saying today, and what in effect I am saying in my motion for the production of papers which I moved at the beginning of the session, is that I believe if meaningful decisions are to be made on this or on any other question, that if the ordinary residents of Prince Edward Island-in this particular case-are to know how such decisions are arrived at, and that if members of Parliament both in government and opposition parties are to be encouraged to reach any sensible conclusions, then surely the fullest information possible must be provided. Otherwise, members of Parliament, and I include government members who are not in the Cabinet as well as opposition members, merely become rubber stamps or ciphers. Without the fullest information on this or any other question, the public cannot be expected to make any meaningful, realistic and sound judgments.
We pride ourselves on living in a democratic society. I say that a democratic system of government cannot really be democratic or function effectively unless and until government, whether federal, provincial or municipal, is prepared to give to the people, who in the final analysis should make the decision, all the information they can properly be given. Of course, there are certain cases where information should be withheld. For example, the government is proposing to build new airports near Montreal and Toronto. The government therefore has the responsibility for purchasing the hundreds of thousands of acres of land which are required for the construction of the modern airports of today. No government could be expected to announce the precise location of such an airport, because to do so would be an invitation to the land speculator to squeeze every dollar he could out of the government. Thus, I recognize there are occasions when the government cannot disclose the details of a particular plan to the members of this House.
In this particular case the government, in its wisdom, made a promise to build a causeway to Prince Edward Island. Much as I disagree with Liberal governments, I cannot believe that this government promise the people of Prince Edward Island that it would build a causeway only because it was thought that in this way some Liberal members from Prince Edward Island might be elected. Even with the feelings I have about the Liberal party and Liberal governments. I cannot believe that. The government must have had some pretty detailed plans and comprehensive cost estimates with regard to the building of this causeway. They must have had some pretty complete documentation and cost benefit ratios in relation to this causeway to back the former government's promise to the people of the Maritimes that the causeway would be built. Later they decided not to build the causeway. I shall leave it to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and others to discuss the details of the causeway since they are much more competent and knowledgeable about it than I.
However, when the government decided not to build the causeway, members of the government must have

April 1, 1971
Prince Edward Island Causeway had all the details concerning what the latest cost-estimate was. They must have had some information concerning the new cost-benefit ratio. Having made the decision first to go ahead, and later not to go ahead, I cannot see any reason why a government which has spoken so often about participatory democracy, a government led by a Prime Minister who so often has said he believes in dialogue or a government which has set up a whole new department, Information Canada, so that ostensibly the people can be told what government departments do and how government decisions are made, should always say no to any request made by any member of Parliament for such information. Unfortunately, it is usually only opposition members who ask for information.
I say this is unfortunate because I believe it indicates that government backbenchers are not doing the work they were elected to do. They function really as office boys for the government instead of members of Parliament. Few, if any, requests for the tabling of documents are agreed to by the government. In this session, as in every other session, there is a long list of motions for the production of papers on every aspect of Canadian life and dealing with questions which are of vital importance either to this country as a whole or to one area. Time after time we get from this arrogant government a simple, flat no. The government will not give to members of Parliament or to the people of Canada the information which they have every right to have. I say to the government that if it believes in the democratic system, if it believes in the kind of participatory democracy about which government members have spoken, if it believes in the right of the ordinary citizen to have all the knowledge he requests in order that he may make the kind of decisions about government policy which one would hope would be made in a democratic society, it should stop functioning within a mantle of secrecy.
The government should face up to the very simple proposition that instead of everything being private, every report, every study made by the government or for a government department should be made public. Then, the people of Canada will know more about those matters in which they are interested and will be able to decide how they should act on the basis of complete information rather than on the basis of the kind of misinformation we so frequently receive in this country when the government says no to the type of request I made in connection with this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be difficult to find a constituency farther from the Prince Edward Island causeway than mine, but perhaps I may be permitted to enter the debate this afternoon for a few minutes as a member representing a coastal constituency. In my province, we have had to deal with island to mainland transportation over many years, so we have had some considerable experience with it. I know that later on the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) will bring to the debate his own firsthand knowledge and his feelings concerning the matter of transportation between his beautiful island and the mainland. I am not altogether unfamiliar with the territory involved. I have taken the trip across on a few occasions. In fact, I took a trip across to the island on one memorable occasion. When I was asked if I would enter the debate this afternoon, I looked up my office diary for 1968 in which I had put down some notes about that trip. I should like to recall them to mind this afternoon. As the scene unfolds it will perhaps become familiar to hon. gentlemen of this House. These diary notes read as follows:
Monday, February 19, 1968. Arrived Moncton about noon. Cold-9 degrees below. Windy. Had lunch and left by bus tor Tormentine to take the ferry to P.E.I. Many cars waiting. Went aboard to find angry crowd held up for hours while we drove from Moncton. Many others including kids and farmers with animals left in the cold. Ferry Abegweit, a 25-year-old railway ferry, all brass and mahogany. Car deck taken up with many rooms down both sides.
There were little brass plaques on the doors. I read the wording on them and noted it in my diary because it was very interesting to see so many rooms and cabins on the car-deck of a ferry which traverses a 9-mile gap. These rooms accommodated pantry stores, crews' mess, carpenter an boatswain stores, engineers' and officers' mess, crews' galley, seamens' mess, provisions stores, waiters, caterer, chief restaurant steward, stewards' smoking room, quartermaster, deckhand, second steward and oilers. The mystery was that any passengers were able to get on board. This was hardly a ferry, I found; it was a floating city which travels between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of New Brunswick.
My notes in the diary continued as follows:
Lots of ice in the strait. Miserable facilities at both ends. Telephones between the terminals have been out of order for two months. Badio on the ship not working. Costs $1.65 to use the ship-to-shore telephone.
Then, the diary note concludes:
Caught in snowbank for seven and a quarter hours and arrived Charlottetown midnight to hear the government had been defeated on its tax legislation.
I have never spent as memorable a night on the ferry services of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker. Let me contrast that with what has taken place in British Columbia. But first, may I say that if I were a regular user of this ferry service, were I a native of P.E.I., I too would be asking for a causeway. As I say, let me contrast that with what has taken place in the province of British Columbia. For many years, stretching back to the early days of the settlements on the west coast, we had a ferry service between the city of Vancouver on the mainland and Victoria on the southern tip of Vancouver Island.
