Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to continue just a little further, you will see how this connects up, and in a very pertinent way, with the motion that is before the House. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) said, we are here to urge the government to make sure that all the considerations were placed before the experts making the survey so that they could make a judgment in respect of the causeway. I think one of the judgments they would want to make, and which the government would want to see them make, is whether or not elimination of the ferry service and the building of a causeway are necessary, simply because there is not a competent ferry system which could be operated in that particular location.
My argument today is that when those documents are tabled, we should have tabled with them a competent examination of the ferry services to determine whether or not a causeway is in the best interests of the people concerned, and whether or not a competent ferry service could give the people what they require. I think that is pertinent to the argument being made, and is narrow enough to adhere to the point that is before the House. If such a study does not come forward with the documents, then I think the government has not properly instructed the experts on carrying out their survey, or the experts themselves have not gone far enough afield in their survey to determine whether or not adequate cost-benefits exist in a causeway. The experts should be prepared to point out other alternatives, and to present documents to the House in order to demonstrate those alternatives.
Following along this argument, I point out that in British Columbia we had experienced a ferry service quite akin to the kind of service that has existed for a long time between P.E.I. and the mainland. That ferry service was operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think this is germane to the argument I am making because in this instance we are speaking of railway operated ferry services. On the west coast, the ferry service grew old. The vessels grew old. The Empress
Prince Edward Island Causeway Hotel in Victoria, one of the famous Canadian hotels, was beginning to run down. The CPR was considering whether or not it could maintain service to the hotel. People began to disregard the ferry service and to use air service. Air service expanded until 17 planes a day were running between Vancouver Island, Schwartz Bay airport and Pat Bay airport serving the city of Victoria.
Eventually, the provincial government decided to build its own ferry service, prompted first of all by completion of a tunnel which enables traffic to move very swiftly out of the heart of Vancouver to the ferry landing area, which is about at the 49th parallel. The ferries are of the most modern kind. They are end loaders. Cars roll off and on with great speed. Fast highways connect the ferry with the two cities at either end, and so what we are looking at, as compared with the former railway service, is a highway oriented ferry system designed to serve automobiles and trucks, and in no way connected with rails. It is based on having excellent highways open at all times for traffic, and fastloading and unloading. This leads one to believe that if a system such as this existed rather than the railway oriented system of Prince Edward Island, it might very well meet the needs of that island, and meet them for a long time, because the Canadian people will have to look at the very, very heavy cost of a causeway to serve that area. If legitimate alternatives exist, then those legitimate alternatives should be explored.
What happened after the highway-oriented service between the mainland and Vancouver Island went into operation? First of all the old Empress Hotel in Vancouver, which the CPR had thought it would have to phase out, suddenly became prosperous and today is being updated to take care of the additional service. Tourism has increased as a result of the improved traffic. What happened to the fast and cheap air service-17 planes a day to the island? The fast highways and fast ferries gave it competition. With the time needed for the drive to the airport, the air flight and the journey at the other end, the demand for air service has decreased to a few planes a day.
In considering the question of a causeway the very large cost involved must be considered. Is it possible that the people of Prince Edward Island would find that their needs could be satisfied with a highway-oriented road service and a ferry service, roads that were open year round to the main points served by the ferry, and terminals adequate to house people in subzero weather? Our experience shows that traffic expands when good service is provided, so there should be good maintenance. Ship-to-shore telephones should remain open, terminal telephones should operate efficiently, and in every way an excellent service should be provided.
If these conditions were made part of the study, I think we could compare this service with the cost of operating a causeway. The people of Prince Edward Island might find that they could have the enjoyment of their island without really connecting it to the mainland by a causeway; that they could have excellent service to and from

Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the ever diligent and thoughtful member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) for taking an interest in this question. I congratulate him for two reasons: a diligent member should be seeking inportant information, especially information relevant to decisions regarding financial expenditures, and I commend him for correctly assessing that this important matter for which the report is requested is not regional or provincial but is a national issue. By bringing forward this motion he reveals himself as a good parliamentarian. I hope the motion will pass.
We are at a stage now where information concerning the causeway project is vitally important. In this respect I should like to refer briefly to the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). I know that his heart is in the right place and that he wishes us well, but I should like to cover a few points where his information might be inadequate.
In Prince Edward Island our greatest cash crop is not readily transportable by truck and so far has required a tremendous movement of reefer cars from the railway. So we are not in a position to abandon the railway at this stage of our economy or technology. I can think of no trucking company which would be in a position to send down the vast number of trucks and transfers required to market such a perishable and market-sensitive product as potatoes.
I would also point out that a comparison of the ferry service in the hon. member's province and mine must include one important ingredient, the fact that we have very heavy ice conditions. For this reason we must have powerful icebreakers to provide continuity and efficiency of service. The hon. member mentioned the ferry boat Abegweit which we crossed on together in 1968-not a luxurious vessel by any means. When one considers how many times that boat has to cross the strait in winter conditions, bucking ice, and that many of these men are on double shift, the fact that they have a little cabin to rest in between shifts cannot be regarded as luxury. It is an old ship, and the people of Prince Edward Island are concerned that it is the only icebreaker that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is leaving with us. It has been in service since 1947. The people are not overjoyed either, with the government's decision to remove the largest and newest car ferry, the John Hamilton Gray.
The people of Canada, and particularly the Maritimes, have been given many conflicting stories about the cost of the Northumberland crossing. I would have thought the government would have welcomed the opportunity to produce this data. At first we were told that the causeway could be built for $105 million, then we were told $146 million. When the project got under way with magnificent spur railways and highways pathetically leading
to the open sea and almost $20 million expended, we were told the cost would be well over $300 million.
When doubt was raised, Colonel Edward Churchill was engaged as a consultant for the Department of Public Works to study the project on the spot, to engage staff to investigate the matter and give an estimate of the cost. Colonel Churchill is a most eminent engineer and was involved in the construction of the Expo site. His recommendations are found in report No. 26 of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, first session of the twenty-eighth Parliament. In answer to a question about the cost of the highway he said, as reported at page 443:
The $300 million figure was not mine, I do not know where it came from, and I think that I cannot make any comment other than to say it is a silly figure. I do not know where it came from.
A diligent member from Prince Edward Island, whose name I will not mention, then asked, "Silly because it is exaggerated?" Colonel Churchill, said "Because it is not true-and it certainly did not come from us." An hon. member then asked, "In your view, is it an exaggerated figure?" Colonel Churchill answered, "Yes." I then said, "Thank you very much." Sir, with this uncertainty, this confusion, this evasion and this repudiation by the government of Canada of a solemn commitment to build a permanent land link, is it any wonder that I should join with great sincerity in the matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North and ask this House for further information on this tremendously important matter?
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North, I am concerned. In the age of Information Canada there seems to be a growing tendency to regard almost any document as being one which should not be revealed. Time after time that is the answer we receive in response to motions for the production of papers. I cannot believe that a democracy can be healthy if it is not informed. Thomas Jefferson enunciated that great truth many years ago. The denial of information surely cannot contribute to the effective and efficient dispatch of our business.
It is particularly important today that we know the true story and what is to be done about the Northumberland crossing. It is important because it may well be in the interests of the financial welfare of Canada that this permanent land link be built now. The particular ferry service which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra talked about is a most expensive service and the subsidy required every year is rising at a rapid rate.
I have always believed, and Colonel Edward Churchill also stated this when being questioned, that it would be good, sound economics to build a permanent land link. If you incur year after year deficits of between $7 million and $10 million, you will soon reach the stage at which a land link, with a toll which would amortize its cost in a reasonable time, will be the better course of economic valour and political wisdom. Yet the people of Prince Edward Island today are uncertain about the cost, despite

April 1, 1971

the fact that the surveying and studying of this great project began in 1956, quite a while ago. Some of the finest experts from three or four countries undertook that study.
Just two days ago I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) if he had received proposals from the government of Prince Edward Island or private interests suggesting that they might build this land link with suitable co-operation from the government of Canada. The minister's answer was no. The press and other media in my province have indicated that such proposals are in the offing. Surely these people must know the financial facts. It is just as important for them to be known by the people for whom decisions are being made.
The people of Prince Edward Island are undergoing a severe diminution in the number of vessels provided for their transportation and for the transportation of their goods between the mainland and our province. The removal of the John Hamilton Gray, our fine, new ferry, was a backward step. So far as winter travel is concerned, we are now back to where we were 20 years ago and depend only on this old boat which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra remembers so well from that stormy night.
It has been a long time since our province entered confederation on the promise that the dominion government would provide us with continuous and efficient transportation to the mainland. It has been a long time since we were reduced to one ship. That is why I believe it is most important for the government to comply with the motion and let the people of Canada, particularly the people of our region, know the facts.

Mr. Speaker, once again I rise to speak on a notice of motion for the production of papers. Frankly, I am surprised how many such motions appear on the order paper. Some hon. members opposite have suggested that this government acts secretly and it does not make information available. That is not in accordance with the facts. There are all sorts of sources of information available to us. I submit that rather than not getting enough information, those of us who want to do a good job are getting a surfeit of material to study. We are inundated with information. It is also not correct to say that none of these papers asked for are produced, because many of them are.
We are dealing with a specific motion in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) which asks for a copy of the report by C.B. Haver of Montreal for Northumberland Consultants Limited on a certain matter. When I read one of these motions for the production of papers of one type or another, my first reaction-I would be less than candid if I did not say this-is, "Why not?". For that reason I have made it a point to listen to reasons advanced by ministers or parliamentary secretaries as to why a particular letter, paper, document, study or report should not be produced.
By the same token, I have paid careful attention to reasons advanced by hon. members for having a certain paper or document produced. Unhappily, many of the reasons advanced by hon. members seem to be lost in
Prince Edward Island Causeway
other comments which they see fit to bootleg into the debate. The comments do not deal specifically with the notice of motion to produce papers but relate to the pet project of the hon. member speaking. I think it is only fair to say that hon. members on this side of the House probably take as much advantage of that opportunity to bootleg remarks into debate as do members of the opposition parties.
Those who have listened to these debates instead of taking part in them have found that some reasons for not producing papers are fairly obvious and are readily acceptable to the mover of the motion. I refer to the situation in which the production of papers, in the opinion of the minister, would affect the security of the nation. To be fair to hon. members moving motions of that kind, almost without exception they agree to withdraw them. Sometimes it is obvious that the hon. member is only fishing. He has heard a rumour or it has been suggested to him that a particular document exists, so he has put on the order paper a notice of motion for the production of the document, only to find when the minister or parliamentary secretary answers that the document does not exist or it is not the property of that minister.
Of course, the other reasons are also advanced by ministers, namely, that the document is a privileged communication between governments or that the federal government or the minister concerned has given the minister or officials of another government an undertaking that such document or documents will be treated as confidential. There are other reasons. This is the grey area into which we get and the reason we have this kind of debate. When a minister receives a report on study, or a document which is needed for internal use of the department, he is called upon to make this decision. He uses this as his reason.
There are times when an individual is asked to prepare a report. That individual, who may be a professor or an expert in a particular field, undertakes the study and reports to cabinet on the understanding that his conclusions will be treated as confidential. If the minister breaks this confidentiality he has broken faith with the individual to whom he has given his word. The minister finds himself in a difficult position. He feels he must honour the undertaking and not reveal the contents of the report because he earlier indicated he would not do so. Surely this is necessary so that the individual who is making the report can feel free to express himself in many areas although he may not be completely in accord with them. He tries out ideas on the minister or department which are, hopefully, backed up by the studies he has made.
Many documents are produced, but not particularly in fulfilment of notices of motions because for one reason or another in the opinion of the minister these documents cannot be produced. Mr. Speaker, the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) relates to a notice of motion for production of papers, namely, the report by Mr. C. B. Haver in connection with the Prince Edward Island causeway. The motion reads:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the report by C. B. Haver of Montreal for Northumberland Consultants Limited regarding a review of the cost-benefit evaluation by Stanford Research Institute for a Prince Edward Island causeway as mentioned in answer to question number 1,832 reported in Hansard July 21, 1969, at page 11374.

Surely it is cabinet ministers and the government who have to make the big decision. If all the working documents prepared for them by civil servants were made public, both the cabinet and the civil servants would be put in an impossible situation. The cabinet has the overall responsibility to decide, whereas the civil servant only has to prepare a report on one specific aspect. The civil servant does not have to take the over-view of what will be the cost of government needs.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North said he was not arguing with the decision that was taken, or the cost of the project, but only the need for these papers to be made public. He argued that members of Parliament must have all information available. Surely this is a time when we want a great deal more background information. When making decisions, we are not prepared to fly blind without the necessary information. In this case the government has made a decision based on the economics of the situation which existed in the spring of 1969. It felt that this was the best course to follow, whether the cost was $140 million or $300 million to which it later escalated. The government had to decide whether it was worth while to spend that amount on that particular project at that time.
When the government decided not to proceed with the project, it announced a development program for the province of Prince Edward Island. The regional development committee met last year and had an opportunity to review with the officials of the province the effect of this program on the province.

The Prime Minister has finally come through with the bonanza that all these fellows have been waiting for for three years. I hope they are able to continue smiling when this bill is passed.

As has been pointed out on several occasions during this and other debates, Canada already pays the highest per capita tax of the countries of the free world. On
Government Organization Act, 1970
looking at part IV and part V of this bill, the first question that came to my mind was: What for? What possible reason could there be, in addition to the present 29 or 30 ministers and with the freedom to appoint an equal number of ministers without portfolio, to want a free hand to appoint an additional five ministers of state at the discretion of the Governor in Council, without consulting Parliament and without necessarily indicating the reason for such appointments.
Part IV states that these ministers will be responsible for formulation and development of policies. If this job is turned over to the ministers of state, what will the existing ministers be doing? What will all the civil service people be doing who are charged with this responsibility? What will the Prime Minister's burgeoning supportive staff be doing? It seems to me that this bill in part IV and part V is proposing to promote a shameful waste of public funds at a time when our economy is in very dire straits as a result of the government's actions. This is not the time to be wasting public funds.
This may be considered an effort by the government to solve in part the unemployment situation, but I wish to point out to the Prime Minister and his gang that the proposed additional ministers are already employed as members of Parliament and there is nothing stopping them assisting ministers on formulation and development of policy as members of Parliament. I cannot see that appointing them as ministers of state would increase their intelligence or their ability to develop and formulate policy.
However, if the government can show me that an appointment such as that would increase the ability of a member to formulate and develop policy, I would suggest all members of Parliament should receive such appointments to the great benefit of the country as a whole. Unfortunately, it appears at present that the great advantage will only be to the majority of Liberal members who will benefit from an extra salary of $15,000 per year. It is very questionable that they will be able to justify such an increased government expenditure.
Mr. Chairman, unless the Prime Minister, in whose name this bill stands, can offer an explanation besides the obvious one, namely, mercenary considerations on behalf of Liberal members, I cannot see any way in which we can support this bill. I would find it much easier to justify a decrease in the size of the cabinet. As an example, the minister responsible for Information Canada cannot really justify the existence of his department to the people of Canada. That department, along with the ministerial post, should be abolished.
The job held by the Secretary of State is hardly one that needs a separate department and minister. That ministerial post could easily be abolished and the department combined with another. The communications ministry could easily be abolished and combined with the Post Office. The three ministers involved in Treasury Board, finance and revenue could easily be cut down to two. The Department of Justice and the Department of the Solicitor General could be joined into one. There are many other examples of too many ministers. When one looks at this bill there are only two possibilities: they are either

I would find it much easier to support this bill if government reorganization were in the direction I am suggesting. That could be much more easily justified to the Canadian people, in view of the massive unemployment and the need to keep government expenditures down in order to reduce taxation. This government has shown a greater and greater desire to turn responsibility over to Crown corporations, thereby decreasing even more the amount of responsibility by individual ministers. That, again, speaks for decreasing rather than increasing the number of ministers.
I also see part IV of this bill as a further effort to downgrade Parliament in law and in reality. The reason for this statement is that ministries of state may be estabished by the Governor in Council, by proclamation, without reference to Parliament. What the Prime Minister is saying, in effect, is that he does not feel Parliament has anything useful to contribute in deciding whether a new ministry should be established, and by this bill he is giving himself the authority to bypass Parliament completely and virtually make the decision on his own. This, along with the rule changes, along with the roster system which allows ministers to be absent from the House half the time, is very telling evidence that the Prime Minister is waging a cold and sinister war against the institution of Parliament.
A year or two ago the government made political capital by suggesting that they would cut down on civil service staff and on their expenditure, yet since that time the bureaucracy has been spreading at an ever-accelerating rate. In the past year the government has also attempted to make political capital from the war on inflation. Nevertheless this bill, which clearly involves a continuing enlargement of the bureaucracy, will vastly increase the inflationary process of this country. As many hon. members have said, part IV of this bill enables between 110 and 130 members on the government side to increase their pay and their status in Parliament. I want you to know, Mr. Chairman, that I object to this surreptitious and underhanded method which hon. members have used for raising their own pay by way of the back door, so to speak.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the invitation of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger), I would like to try to speak as honestly as possible.
The committee of the whole is studying clause 14 of bill C-207 entitled "An Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto."
I will therefore limit my comments to this clause.
Mr. Chairman, I would like, for the information of my hon. colleagues, to divide clause 14 into four parts, and analyze them one by one.
Here is what the first part of clause 14 stipulates: Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters-
Mr. Chairman, that is to say that the first part of clause 14 which I just quoted indicates the government's purpose which is to meet requirements of new policies to

April 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
be formulated. In fact, it will be noted, that part of clause 14 refers to requirements -for formulating and developing new policies-
Mr. Chairman, we agree that new policies must be adopted. No member will deny that. Besides, the problem is not at that level. There is no reference in this first part to the implementation of these policies nor to what they will involve. The only reason given to justify the establishment of these new ministries of state is that there are -requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies-
What is a new and comprehensive policy? What does it involve? What problems does it correspond to?
Mr. Chairman, clause 14 contains no reply either in the letter or in the spirit. There is no reference to implementation of new policies. Only formulation and development are mentioned.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, only studies, analyses or inquiries are referred to.
In other words, they will create a ministry headed by a minister who will make studies, analyses, surveys, develop a new policy, but will not administer them and will not take measures to solve a specific problem. They will be content with conducting studies.
Mr. Chairman, this is, in elusive terms, a judicial mess which cannot satisfy hon. members. This is why we are having this debate which we would like to be constructive.
The first part of clause 14 does not justify the establishment of ministers and ministries of state, this is merely eye-wash. The purpose of clause 14, the very principle of the creation of five new ministries and five new ministers of state is the following: "formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies".
Mr. Chairman, it is regrettable that there is no mention of application, that there is no specification of what is meant. Furthermore, none of the government members have given us this information. To oblige them, to speed up the work, we should vote blindly. No, Mr. Chairman. One may accept the principle of the formulation of "new policies" but at the same time one must not be afraid to ask for information. The clause does not specify either in what fields exactly such new policies will be formulated; it only states that policies will be formulated, that such policies will have to be new and comprehensive.
Mr. Chairman, would this mean that, through this clause, the government admits that its present policy is old-fashioned and unintelligible? I would not go so far as to say that, but why speak of a new and comprehensive policy if the government is unable to justify it?
We must also note, Mr. Chairman, that the first part of clause 14 does not specify the number of areas referred to. No general indication is given about the areas which would need a new and comprehensive policy; it is only stated that it will be related to one or several matters.
Indeed, the second part of clause 14 reads as follows:
_the requirements for formulating and developing new and
comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters-

.. .warrant the establishment of a "special portion". No reference is made to a normal portion usually found in a normal department, but a "special portion". What does "special portion" mean? What is this new invention of the government?
Mr. Chairman, we do not get an answer to the question either:
-presided over by a Minister

There is the second part of clause 14. In short, in the second part of clause 14, there is a question of establishing "a special portion.. .presided over by a Minister". Does it mean that this minister will have a special status, compared to other ministers? It would matter greatly to get an answer to this question.
What will be the relationship between the House and the ministers who will preside over a special portion? And will this agency constitute a crown corporation with mixed participation, or a mandatory crown corporation? Will it be merely a ministry of state? Or rather a sort of make-believe ministry, not responsible to parliament?
Mr. Chairman, I have no preconceived opinion on this question. I am merely asking it. We are expecting an answer.
So we want to establish, to face a special "portion", a ministry presided over by a minister. Why then this "special portion"? What can justify the development of a special policy in Canada? What is this? To put it in a nutshell, in the second part of clause 14 we are told that a "special portion" will be presided over by a minister of state. This is therefore an excuse as the first part of the clause does not say what this new and comprehensive policy consists of. We are not told either what is meant by a "special portion". We cannot guess why a minister should be put in charge of such a service.
This is why we will fiercely oppose the passing of this part of Bill C-207 as long as the government does not specify its intentions in this regard, because as far as we are concerned this is a foolish and unjustified way of spending public funds.
Mr. Chairman, if the government leaves us in the dark because it does not know what is going on, we must conclude that this part of the bill is in fact a pretext to designate ministers of state.
I am still on clause 14 part of which reads as follows:
-a Minister charged with responsibility for formulation and development of such policies-
Not for their implementation, Mr. Chairman! It is not said:	"a Minister charged with responsibility for
implementation of such policies". No. There is no mention of implementation, no talk of translating words into action. Nothing is said of tackling specific problems in particular areas. The clause merely states that the minister designated to preside over the ministry will be charged with the sole responsibility and function of formulating and developping "new and comprehensive policies".
Why "new and comprehensive policies"? What does this responsibility consist of? Does that mean that the
April 1, 1971

ministers responsible for those ministries will have absolutely no influence on present policy and administration? Mr. Chairman, that is obviously what this clause would have us believe.
Mention should at least be made in this clause of application. On the contrary, it speaks merely of "formulating and developing policies".
To understand clearly what the responsibilities of the minister will be, let us go back to the first part of clause 14 and find out why a ministry is to be set up. No reason is given. This may enlighten us with regard to the responsibilities of the minister!
I quote once more from the first part of the clause:
-the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters-
This is the purpose to achieve. This is the justification for appointing a minister of state and for creating five new ministries, and thanks to this obscure wording, a minister will be appointed who will have no power to influence policies directly but who will only have the power to study.
Mr. Chairman, to conclude this rapid analysis, I should like now that we consider this part of clause 14, and I quote:
-the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a ministry of State for that purpose.
Because "new and comprehensive policies" have to be drawn up, so says the government, a minister will be appointed at the head of a department, the so-called "special portion". Who is going to create the department? Who is going to appoint the minister?
Mr. Chairman, not parliament, not you, nor I, nor hon. members opposite either, nor my own colleagues. Who then? The people's representatives? No, Mr. Chairman. Clause 14 states clearly and I repeat:
-the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
This means the cabinet will create those departments and appoint those ministers. It will not need the authority of the House. All the Prime Minister needs to do is to convene the cabinet, establish the Ministry of State, give it a name and hand a reward to a new minister without coming before the institution that controls the taxpayers' money, namely Parliament.
Mr. Chairman, this is an infringement of our democratic system, a direct blow to Parliament which is entitled to scrutinize the administration of the country.
And I would use the same language if the Progressive Conservative party or the New Democratic party were in office. A principle is at stake. Will Parliament exercise control on the establishment of those ministries and ministers of state? If not, why should the government ignore Parliament when, last year or the year before, it did consult it to establish other departments? Why, at the present time, should some ministers be appointed without the agreement of the House, whereas others could not be appointed in such conditions? That is already unfair to the 29 other ministers who have submitted to the will of
Government Organization Act, 1970
the House. Why a preferred treatment for some, while others will have to abide by the democratic requirements of this institution?
Mr. Chairman, if we get no answer to that question, we are entitled to believe two things. The first is that the government does not care about Parliament, and the second is that the government wishes to hurry to appoint certain persons to positions which will mean for them a title and a higher allowance.
Mr. Chairman, here is then in my opinion an indirect way to vote oneself a $15,000 yearly increase over and above one's allowance.
Mr. Chairman, I am quite puzzled by the fact that the government refuses to consult Parliament.
This is why I am proposing, supported by the member for Roberval (M. Gauthier), the following amendment to clause 14, in view of the explanation and of the analysis I have just made:
That clause 14 of the Act respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto be amended by striking out lines 22 to 24 and substituting therefor:
"Parliament may pass an Act amending the Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and having the effect of creating a Ministry of State."
Mr. Chairman, it will be noted that in this amendment I am respecting the government's wish to create more ministries of state. But, as a member of Parliament, I request the government to respect this supreme institution and to submit to Parliament any decision aimed at setting up any ministry of state since Parliament is the sole body in a position to decide on the establishment of a ministry of state.
I find this request reasonable and honest. The member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) who, a few moments ago, appealed to our honesty can testify to it. He cannot say now that I am guilty of partisan politics.
Mr. Chairman, I think that this is a serious and positive proposal. It may be read in the bill that:
-the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
I wish it would be written instead: parliament may establish a ministry of state. Why should there be an exceptional situation in the case of some ministries of state, while all other ministers, when their departments were established, had to face parliament?
Mr. Chairman, this is an illogic thing, unacceptable to parliament. This why there are pretty stormy debates now in this House, and I think it is normal, understandable and important.
I therefore table a copy of this amendment.

full meaning of the bill and I thought I would help them a little and cover some of the ground that had been covered previously. I apologize if I seem to have wandered to some extent. It seemed to me that the hon. member for Mercier also wandered a little in his remarks.
It is an old trick for a government, when it runs into a messy sort of situation such as exists today, to try to diffuse responsibility as much as possible. Under the term of this bill some 110 members may hold positions of one kind or another. That is a tremendous diffusion of responsibility. It is very useful to be able to say, "That isn't quite in my department. See the chap in the other office about it," or to say, "That fellow is out of town." I imagine if you had 110 people either serving in the cabinet or as parliamentary secretaries, at least 30 or 40 of them would be out of town at any one time. This would make it difficult to pin down where responsibility lay.
I have been told of a situation in one department in Ottawa where there are people who make their living simply by moving the position of papers in files. Requests and documents build up over the years. The person responsible takes the ones from the bottom of the pile and places them on top. It is just like shuffling a deck of cards. For some people it may mean that their requests, scheduled to be dealt with in six months' time, can be handled in a matter of weeks.
I believe it was the hon. member for St. John's East who commented on Information Canada. It is a new department and provides a parallel with the proposed ministries of state. Some weeks ago a document came into my office from Information Canada enumerating all that Information Canada had done. I do not have it with me but it said something to the effect: We had four letters on this subject and three letters on that subject. It listed about 28 or 30 letters and I understood that was the total number of requests for information it had received. Probably Information Canada was busy answering those letters. I presume it also produces the glossy reprints of minister's speeches, sends them across the country and sees that they reach Members of Parliament. But the sum total of work enumerated did not amount to any more correspondence than would go through a Member of Parliament's office in the course of half a day. Most of us thought that Information Canada would receive a flood of mail.
The subject of committee meetings has been mentioned in this debate. I wish to give an example of one committee meeting. A week or two ago I walked into a meeting of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee. There were three or four members present, sitting, dozing, and listening to evidence. They were passing millions of dollars worth of estimates and were actually sitting around dozing as if they did not have any responsibility. I only wish the people who voted for them could have seen what was happening.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ISRAEL1-ARAB CONFLICT-SUGGESTED REPRESENTATIONS TO ISRAEL RESPECTING PEACE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
At a meeting of parliamentarians in Cairo a few months ago I said that I believed Israel had the right to exist. That aspect of my remarks was not very popular. I went on to say that it did not have the right to exist within boundaries of its own choosing. Surely within these parameters there is still an opportunity for us to do useful work. Surely we can show more interest, be more helpful and generous and do something to assist in brightening the currently faint lamp of peace in this vital and crucial area.
Hon, Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for giving me the opportunity
of saying a word about the Canadian position on this grave Middle East situation. The present stage of efforts to make progress toward a lasting Middle East peace settlement involves both continuing dangers and challenging opportunities. The absence since March 7 of formal and mutual agreements to maintain the cease-fire underlines the persisting risk that hostilities might at some point be renewed unless the momentum of the current peace initiative is maintained and reinforced. But there are encouraging possibilities for such progress toward peace which I hope will be taken up and exploited by the parties.
The government of Canada has followed with close interest the latest sequence of exchanges under the aegis of Ambassador Jarring, the United Nations Secretary General's special representative charged with promoting a peace settlement on the basis of Resolution 242 which, as the hon. member for Hillsborough has reminded us, was drafted with the help of Canada which was then on the Security Council. Although Canada is not directly involved in these efforts and we are, therefore, not informed of all aspects of the exchanges, certain observations can fairly be made on the basis of development known to us.
I should like first to reiterate the Canadian government's full support of Ambassador Jarring's persistent and untiring efforts to assist the parties toward a settlement based on the Security Council resolution. The House is well aware of the formidable nature of the issues to be resolved. Any expectation of rapid advance toward agreement would be illusory. But some encouragement may be drawn from the Secretary General's report of March 5 on the course of Ambassador Jarring's mission.
In drawing attention to the intensity of recent efforts to move toward a peaceful solution, the Secretary General noted that general agreement had been found on some of the problems to be settled. He also cited with satisfaction the positive reply given by the United Arab Republic on specific questions raised by Ambassador Jarring. As the House is aware, the UAR response included an explicit expression of readiness to enter into a peace agreement with Israel subject, of course, to mutually acceptable terms of such agreement being worked out. At the same time, the Secretary General has appealed to the government of Israel to respond favourably to Ambassador Jarring's initiative. Ambassador Jarring will doubtless seek
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
now to elaborate progressively the terms of a peace settlement. For this he will be dependent upon good will and restraint by the parties in asserting what they see as their respective vital interests.
In the Canadian government's view, the essential basis for a just and lasting peace remains available to the parties in the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 242. The opportunity is theirs, with Ambassador Jarring's help, to resolve within that framework all their outstanding differences. In this respect, the response of the UAR government to the questions posed by Ambassador Jarring is encouraging. We earnestly hope that the ultimate effort will be made along these lines, as a matter of urgency, to convert the present absence of hostilities into an enduring peace.
The Canadian government's concern to see the exchanges under Ambassador Jarring proceed successfully has been emphasized to the parties in these terms in our regular diplomatic contacts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday I directed the following question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro):
Has the government come to any decision or is it in the process of negotiating a cost-sharing agreement with the provinces or with any province with respect to any of the several paramedical services?
The minister gave a negative reply to my question. This same question was raised about five months ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Mac-Innis) and myself. At the time, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Isabelle) indicated in part of his reply that in 1969 several provincial ministers had asked the federal government to include some paramedical services in the national scheme. He said it was up to the government to take a decision in this matter and not up to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
He also indicated that the minister had informed the provincial health ministers that he was prepared to discuss with the cabinet the inclusion of some services as soon as the provinces and territories had set a date for joining the national plan. He indicated that the minister intends to draw the attention of the other cabinet members to this important matter in due course.
There is no doubt that the government has conveniently forgotten that the Medical Care Act permits the inclusion of paramedical services. This section was added to the act by amendment on December 6, 1966. In the debate on the amendment it was made crystal clear that any province would be able to go ahead with providing additional services provided, of course, that the minister and the Governor in Council agree. This certainly is not the interpretation which the minister and this government currently places on the legislation. There is no need to obtain a consensus from the provinces, and there is no provision which says that all provinces must agree before cost-sharing arrangements can be made with a province.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the construction the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has put on the proposed amendment is correct, namely, that it would be possible for one or any number of provinces to admit any health services. I want to assure the committee that the amendment proposed is not a pious wish.
Here we have the present government House leader, who was Minister of National Health and Welfare at that time, giving a solemn commitment that paramedical services could be instituted by a single province. This certainly is not the interpretation which is currently being placed on the Medical Care Act.
Over the past few months members of this House have received an increasing number of requests from individuals and organizations urging that paramedical services be included as a cost-shared item under the medical care program. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the health of the Canadian people should be one of the prime objectives of any government. In many thousands of cases, paramedical services are the only type of health care which an individual requires, and I feel they should be his or hers by right under the various provincial acts. There is no reason why the government should further delay allowing those provinces which wish to include these services, but can only include them if they are based on a costsharing basis with the federal government, to do so.
I understand that most provinces in Canada have already indicated that they intend to institute a medical care program. There should be no further delay by this government and by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in dealing with this matter. I trust that before this session is over the Canadian people will receive the welcome news that paramedical services will be part of the cost-sharing program under our Medical Care Act.

Mr. Speaker, to answer in a more elaborate manner the question of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), i.e. if the government has taken a decision, or if negotiations are presently taking place with some provinces about paramedical services, here are in a few words the facts of the situation.
At the meeting of Ministers of Health in November 1968, this question was studied. Some provinces were then of the opinion that it would be wise not to proceed too quickly with the expansion of benefits, before acquiring some experience on the operation of provincial plans. At that time, the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) promised that the federal government would not apply the provisions of paragraph (3) of section 4 of the Medical Care Act to any supplementary health service, as long as there was not unanimous consent of all the provinces and territories, and as long as the effective date of all plans, in the provinces and territories, was not known.
At the ministers' conference of November 1969, these provinces showed a much more confident attitude, and a formal request was made towards optometry services. As will be remembered, the minister stated that he would discuss the matter with his colleagues, when all the provinces and territories had made known the date of their adhesion to the federal medical care programme.
At the December, 1970, conference, the provinces agreed on the fact that no expansion of services would take place before the results of the review of the financial cost sharing arrangements were known.
I hope that some hon. members will understand that if the government takes the lead in this field, the provinces must also do their share.
